# Lohicca Sutta (DN 12 (PTS DN i 224))

**ID:** DN 12 (PTS DN i 224)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Lohicca Sutta* (DN 12) is the twelfth discourse of the *Dīghanikāya* and belongs to the *Sīlakkhandhavagga* [Gethin 2001; Hazra 1994]. Set at Sālavatikā—a royal domain under King Pasenadi of Kosala granted to the brahmin Lohicca—the discourse centers on Lohicca's pernicious view (*pāpakaṁ diṭṭhigataṁ*) that an ascetic or brahmin who has attained a wholesome doctrine should not teach it to others [Walshe 1987; Jennings 1948; Seeger 2005]. Lohicca reasoned that one person cannot do anything for another, comparing the declaration of the doctrine to binding a new fetter after cutting an old one [Walshe 1987; Seeger 2005; Shih You Xin 2009]. After Lohicca sends his barber Bhesika to invite the Buddha for a meal, the Buddha visits his residence and engages him in a dialogue on the ethics of teaching [Walshe 1987; Allon 1997; Humphreys 1956]. The Buddha refutes Lohicca's reasoning with analogies, showing that a teacher withholding instruction acts destructively toward prospective disciples, and delineates three types of blameworthy teachers in contrast to blameless teachers [Humphreys 1956; Hazra 1994; Shih You Xin 2009]. The sutta then rehearses the standard sequential path of training and spiritual attainments shared with the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* (DN 2), though without explicitly dividing it into three separate categories [Gethin 2001; Hazra 1994; Gethin 2008].

 The text is also cited in the *Mahāniddesa* (Mnd 14) and *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 10.3, Kv 18.9). DharmaNexus computed alignments confirm extensive Pali-internal text reuse with Vinaya narrative material (Kd 1, Kd 6, Kd 15), other *Sīlakkhandhavagga* discourses (notably DN 3, DN 4, DN 5), and collections in the *Aṅguttaranikāya* (AN 2, AN 3, AN 4, AN 5, AN 8) [DharmaNexus]. Cross-language alignments automatically detected by DharmaNexus connect portions of the sutta with the Chinese *Dīrgha-āgama* (T 1), *Madhyama-āgama* (T 26), and *Saṃyuktāgama* (T 99), as well as the Sanskrit *Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra* and sections of the Tibetan *Vinayavibhaṅga* and *Vinayavastu* [DharmaNexus].
